simFastBOIN

Simulation tools for Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) designs in phase I dose-finding trials. The documentation, with the seven vignettes, is also available at https://gosukehommaex.github.io/simFastBOIN/, with a cheat sheet of the functions and articles on how the package is checked and on its computation time.

Overview

simFastBOIN tabulates the BOIN decision boundaries, simulates the design to obtain operating characteristics, and applies the MTD selection rule used at the end of a trial. The simulation engine is written in C++.

The engine draws one uniform variate per patient, in enrollment order, and applies the decision rules in the same order as BOIN::get.oc(). With the same seed and matching arguments the two implementations agree trial by trial, not merely on average. The test suite checks this directly against the BOIN package rather than relying on a tolerance, so the claim is verifiable rather than asserted. A wider comparison ships with the package as inst/validation/compare-with-BOIN.R, which runs 200 configurations covering every combination of the options the two packages share, including extrasafe and titration.

Version 2.1.0 adds the time-to-event BOIN (TITE-BOIN) design, for toxicity that appears late in the assessment window or accrual that outpaces it. New patients are treated while earlier ones are still being followed, with the pending outcomes handled either by the single mean imputation of Yuan et al. (2018) or by the effective sample size of Lin and Yuan (2020). The decision table reproduces the published tables of Yuan et al. (2018) entry by entry, and whenever no patient is pending the simulated trials are identical to those of sim_boin() with the same seed.

The same version adds backfilling: patients who arrive while the dose escalation waits are treated at a lower dose that is safe and has shown a response. BF-BOIN (Zhao et al., 2024) backfills around the BOIN design, and BE-BOIN (Chen et al., 2026) around the time-to-event design. The operating characteristics of Table 4 of Zhao et al. (2024) are reproduced within simulation error.

For trials of two drugs given together, the same version adds the BOIN drug-combination design of Lin and Yin (2017), which looks for an MTD combination in a matrix of doses. It follows BOIN::get.oc.comb() trial by trial and reproduces the example of Yan et al. (2020) to the printed precision.

Version 2.2.0 adds the BOIN-ET design of Takeda et al. (2018), which decides from both the DLT and the response and selects the optimal biological dose (OBD), with its time-to-event (TITE-BOIN-ET) and backfill (BF-BOIN-ET) versions. The boundaries and the decision table of Takeda et al. (2018) are reproduced exactly, and the operating characteristics agree within simulation error with those of the ‘boinet’ and ‘bfboinet’ packages of the authors.

The same version adds the BOIN12 design of Lin et al. (2020), which treats each cohort at the dose with the most desirable balance of response and toxicity, measured by a utility. Its desirability score table reproduces Table 3 of the article in all 166 cells, and its engine agrees trial by trial with a separate Python implementation. The titration of the BOIN design can now stop at a given dose, which with an early stop at six patients gives the accelerated BOIN design of Kojima et al. (2024).

Its time-to-event version, TITE-BOIN12 (Zhou et al., 2022), treats new patients while the DLT or the response of earlier patients is still pending, which shortens the trial; when every decision waits for all the outcomes it gives exactly the trials of BOIN12.

Comb-BOIN12 (Lu et al., 2025) extends BOIN12 to two drugs given together and selects the optimal biological dose combination with a logistic model of the response. With one row of combinations its trials are those of BOIN12. TITE-Comb-BOIN12 applies its rules at the decision times of TITE-BOIN12. BOIN-ETC (Kakizume et al., 2024) divides the dose matrix of two drugs into subtrials along which the toxicity increases, runs BOIN-ET in each of them and selects the optimal dose combination by a utility, in the three versions of the article.

Version 2.3.0 adds six designs. Two extend the single-agent design: the iBOIN design of Zhou et al. (2021) brings prior information, a skeleton of prior DLT probabilities and a prior effective sample size, into the decision boundaries, which then depend on the dose; iboin_boundary() reproduces Table 1 of the article, and without prior information the trials are those of sim_boin(). The gBOIN design of Mu et al. (2019) decides from toxicity grades that carry scores, such as the equivalent toxicity score, instead of from the DLT alone; with the two scores 0 and 1 its trials are those of sim_boin(). The gBOIN-ET design of Takeda et al. (2022) does the same for the optimal biological dose: toxicity grades and efficacy grades carry scores, and the mean scores take the place of the DLT and response rates of BOIN-ET (sim_gboin_et()). Its time-to-event version, TITE-gBOIN-ET (Takeda et al., 2023), enrolls the next cohort while earlier patients are still assessed (sim_tite_gboin_et()). For two drugs given together, the waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016) finds the MTD contour, one MTD at every dose level of one of the drugs, by a sequence of single-agent BOIN subtrials (sim_waterfall()); it follows BOIN::get.oc.comb() with mtd.contour = TRUE. The U-BOIN design of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019) finds the optimal biological dose from the posterior mean utility of the joint outcome of a patient, after a first stage that runs as the BOIN design (sim_uboin()).

Each of these designs is compared with the tables of its article and, where one exists, with a reference implementation in another R package, and its engine agrees trial by trial with a separate implementation in Python; the sections below give the results.

For every design but the waterfall design, oc_scenarios(), oc_results() and oc_compare() set the operating characteristics of several designs and scenarios side by side and judge them against the true MTDs and OBDs, with print() and plot() methods; vignette("simFastBOIN-comparison") applies them to every family of designs.

Installation 

install.packages("simFastBOIN")

Or the development version:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gosukehommaEX/simFastBOIN")

Since version 2.0.0 the package contains compiled code, so a working C++ toolchain is needed to install from source (Rtools on Windows, Xcode command line tools on macOS).

Quick start 

library(simFastBOIN)

oc <- sim_boin(
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 10000,
  seed = 123
)

oc

Compare several dose-toxicity scenarios under the same design:

sim_boin_multi(
  target = 0.30,
  scenarios = list(
    "MTD at dose 2"   = c(0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75),
    "MTD at dose 4"   = c(0.02, 0.06, 0.15, 0.30, 0.50),
    "All doses toxic" = c(0.40, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85)
  ),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 10000,
  seed = 123
)

Look at the boundaries the design will actually use:

print(boin_boundary(target = 0.30, max_n = 18, extrasafe = TRUE), cohort_size = 3)

Read the dose decisions off a table, or off a figure for a protocol:

decisions <- boin_decision_table(target = 0.30, max_n = 18)

print(decisions, cohort_size = 3)
plot(decisions)                      # needs ggplot2

When toxicity can appear late, or patients arrive faster than they can be assessed, use the time-to-event design. Its decisions also depend on how long the pending patients have been followed:

tite <- tite_boin_decision_table(target = 0.30, max_n = 15)
print(tite, cohort_size = 3)

sim_tite_boin(
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  window = 3,          # a three month assessment window
  accrual_rate = 2,    # two patients a month
  n_trials = 10000,
  seed = 123
)

To backfill patients to lower doses while the escalation waits, give the response probabilities as well:

sim_bf_boin(
  target = 0.25,
  p_true = c(0.04, 0.12, 0.25, 0.43, 0.63),
  p_resp = c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.58),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  window = 1,          # a one month assessment window
  accrual_rate = 3,    # three patients a month
  n_earlystop = 9,
  n_trials = 10000,
  seed = 123
)

For two drugs given together, give the true DLT rates as a matrix, with the levels of drug A in the rows and those of drug B in the columns:

sim_comb_boin(
  target = 0.25,
  p_true = matrix(c(0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.14,
                    0.08, 0.25, 0.42, 0.48,
                    0.25, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  n_cohort = 16,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 10000,
  seed = 123
)

Design options

Argument Effect
titration Treat one patient per dose until the first DLT, then switch to full cohorts
titration_doses Stop the titration at this dose; with n_earlystop = 6, the accelerated BOIN design of Kojima et al. (2024)
extrasafe Add a stopping rule at the lowest dose that triggers before elimination
bound_mtd Refuse to select a dose whose estimate exceeds the de-escalation boundary
n_earlystop Stop once the current dose has accrued this many patients and the design would stay
start_dose Dose level for the first cohort, ignored under titration
stay_on_1_of_3 Make one DLT out of three a stay rather than a de-escalation
min_mtd_sample Smallest number of patients for a dose to be eligible as the MTD

Note that n_earlystop defaults to 18 here, whereas BOIN::get.oc() defaults to 100, which in practice switches the rule off. Set it explicitly when comparing the two.

Prior information: the iBOIN design

The iBOIN design of Zhou et al. (2021) brings prior information on the DLT probability of every dose, a skeleton and a prior effective sample size, into the decision boundaries, which then depend on the dose and approach those of the BOIN design as patients are treated there. Dose elimination and the safety stopping rule keep the uniform prior of the BOIN design, so that a misleading skeleton cannot weaken them.

iboin_boundary(target = 0.30, skeleton = c(0.10, 0.19, 0.30, 0.42, 0.54),
               prior_ess = 3, max_n = 30)

oc <- sim_iboin(
  target = 0.30, p_true = c(0.08, 0.15, 0.31, 0.45, 0.55),
  skeleton = c(0.10, 0.19, 0.30, 0.42, 0.54), prior_ess = 3,
  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 100, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

The article gives two ways to select the MTD, with and without the prior information, and does not say which one its simulations use; they are reproduced with the prior information, the default (select_with_prior). robust = TRUE gives the robust prior of the article. Without prior information the trials are those of sim_boin() for the same seed.

How the implementation is checked:

  • iboin_boundary() reproduces the 100 boundaries of Table 1 of Zhou et al.
    1. exactly, and inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2021.R sets the simulations beside the rows BOIN, iBOIN and iBOINR of Table S.1 of its supporting information: 144 of the 150 values lie within simulation error, and the other six, the percentage of patients above the MTD in two scenarios, are explained by the definition of that published quantity.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, fed with the same random numbers.

Toxicity grades: the gBOIN design

The gBOIN design of Mu et al. (2019) decides from toxicity grades that carry scores, such as the equivalent toxicity score, instead of from the DLT alone. The scores are divided by their maximum, and the mean score at the current dose is compared with the boundaries of the BOIN design; the target is on the same scale.

p_grade <- rbind(                      # grades 0 or 1, 2, 3 and 4
  c(0.83, 0.75, 0.62, 0.51, 0.34, 0.19),
  c(0.12, 0.15, 0.18, 0.19, 0.16, 0.11),
  c(0.04, 0.07, 0.11, 0.14, 0.15, 0.11),
  c(0.01, 0.03, 0.09, 0.16, 0.35, 0.59)
)
oc <- sim_gboin(
  target = 0.47 / 1.5, p_grade = p_grade, score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5),
  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 100, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

A dose is eliminated when the posterior probability that its mean score exceeds the target is above the cutoff (elim_rule = "posterior", the rule of the article); elim_rule = "count" applies the elimination boundary of the number of DLTs to the total score, as the ‘UnifiedDoseFinding’ package does. With two categories scored 0 and 1 the trials are those of sim_boin() for the same seed.

How the implementation is checked:

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Mu2019.R reproduces the 14 boundaries of Table 2 of Mu et al. (2019) and sets the simulations beside its Table 5: 101 of the 120 cells lie within simulation error, three hold misprints, and 16 do not agree for a reason that was not found; 13 of these lie outside the allowance also for the values of the ‘UnifiedDoseFinding’ package.
  • With elim_rule = "count", all 130 values of inst/validation/compare-with-UnifiedDoseFinding.R agree with that package within simulation error.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, fed with the same random numbers.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-introduction") for both designs.

Late-onset toxicity: the TITE-BOIN design

method Pending outcomes handled by Boundaries refer to Default suspension rule
"imputation" Single mean imputation (Yuan et al., 2018) STFT Suspend accrual when more than half of the patients at the dose are pending
"ess" Effective sample size (Lin and Yuan, 2020) ESS Escalate only once two patients at the dose have completed the assessment

STFT is the total follow-up time of the pending patients divided by the length of the assessment window, and ESS adds to it the number of patients who have completed the assessment. Neither table depends on the length of the window. Both suspension rules can be set for either method with max_pending_ratio and min_completed.

A simulation needs the length of the window and the accrual rate in the same unit of time. Arrivals can be exponential (the default), uniform or fixed, and the time to DLT Weibull, with a share late_fraction of the DLTs in the second half of the window, or uniform. The follow-up of the pending patients can be weighted by a piecewise uniform prior for the time to DLT through prior_weights; both articles evaluate their designs with equal weights, the default.

How the implementation is checked:

  • tite_boin_decision_table() reproduces all 640 entries of Table 1 (target 0.2) of Yuan et al. (2018) and of Table S1 (target 0.3) of its supplementary appendix, and the dose decisions of the trial example in Figure 1 of that article. The published tables allow de-escalation when the observed DLT rate equals the target, which equation (5) of the appendix, read literally, does not; the package follows the tables.
  • With no patient pending at any decision, the trials of tite_boin_simulate() and the summaries of sim_tite_boin() are identical to those of boin_simulate() and sim_boin() under the same seed.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python and run on a replica of R’s random number stream.

Neither article reports operating characteristics that can be reproduced number for number: Yuan et al. (2018) give them as figures relative to the 3+3 design and as averages over randomly generated scenarios, and the tables of Lin and Yuan (2020) are for the keyboard and mTPI designs.

Backfilling: BF-BOIN and BE-BOIN

In BF-BOIN the dose escalation proceeds in fully staggered cohorts with the BOIN decision table. A patient who arrives while it waits is backfilled to the highest lower dose that has not been eliminated, has fewer than n_cap patients and has a response observed at or below it. Backfilled doses whose DLT rate becomes too high are closed, and when their data conflict with those of the current dose the escalation decides from the pooled data. BE-BOIN applies the same rules around the time-to-event design, with the suspension rules of Chen et al. (2025), and imputes the pending patients in every estimate. The MTD is selected from all patients, backfilled ones included.

Where the articles leave a detail of the simulation open, the package offers an argument: no_slot (a patient with nowhere to go waits or is turned away), conflict_dose (which conflicting dose anchors the pooled estimate) and resp_window, resp_late_fraction and resp_cor (the timing of responses and their correlation with DLTs).

How the implementation is checked:

  • The operating characteristics of Table 4 of Zhao et al. (2024), twelve scenarios of BF-BOIN and five of BOIN, are reproduced within simulation error, durations included, with stay_on_1_of_3 = TRUE, n_earlystop = 9, accrual = "uniform" and no_slot = "leave". The script inst/validation/compare-with-Zhao2024.R repeats the comparison.
  • The trial examples of Zhao et al. (2024) and Chen et al. (2026) are replayed patient by patient.
  • When no dose is opened for backfilling the trials are identical to those of boin_simulate() and tite_boin_simulate() under the same seed.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python and run on a replica of R’s random number stream.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-backfill") for the rules, the choices made where the articles are silent, and the comparison with Table 4.

Drug combinations

sim_comb_boin() implements the design of Lin and Yin (2017) as the BOIN package does in BOIN::get.oc.comb() with mtd.contour = FALSE, including the details that the package adds to the article: a candidate’s posterior probability is increased by 0.0005 per patient treated there, the trial can stop at n_earlystop, and the MTD is selected from (y + 0.05) / (n + 0.1) smoothed by Iso::biviso(). Note that n_earlystop defaults to 18 here, whereas BOIN::get.oc.comb() defaults to 100.

How the implementation is checked:

  • The example of Yan et al. (2020) is reproduced to the printed precision. The one average exactly half-way between two printed values, 1.905 patients at A2B4, is printed 1.90 in the article and 1.91 by R 4.6.0.
  • With the same seed, the results equal those of BOIN::get.oc.comb() exactly; the tests check nine settings, and inst/validation/compare-comb-with-BOIN.R 200 configurations.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python and run on a replica of R’s random number stream.
  • inst/validation/compare-with-LinYin2017.R sets the results beside Tables 2 and 3 of Lin and Yin (2017), whose rules differ in some details.

To run a trial, comb_boin_next() gives the combination for the next cohort from the numbers of patients and DLTs observed so far. It takes its decision with the same C++ code as the simulations, so the trial follows the rules whose operating characteristics sim_comb_boin() reports. BOIN::next.comb() differs from the simulations of BOIN::get.oc.comb() in a few rules, which the help page of comb_boin_next() lists.

nxt <- comb_boin_next(
  target = 0.25,
  n_pts = matrix(c(6, 6, 0, 0,
                   3, 3, 0, 0,
                   0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  n_tox = matrix(c(0, 1, 0, 0,
                   1, 2, 0, 0,
                   0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  current = c(2, 2)
)
nxt        # de-escalate to A1B2
plot(nxt)  # the dose matrix with the data and the decision

See vignette("simFastBOIN-combination").

The MTD contour: the waterfall design

Several combinations of two drugs can have a DLT probability close to the target. The waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016) looks for the MTD contour, one MTD at every dose level of drug A, by dividing the dose matrix into subtrials run with the single-agent BOIN design. sim_waterfall() follows BOIN::get.oc.comb() with mtd.contour = TRUE, the implementation of the authors in the BOIN package, including four rules that the article does not describe and that the help page lists.

p_true <- matrix(c(0.01, 0.04, 0.11, 0.15, 0.30,
                   0.03, 0.05, 0.13, 0.30, 0.50,
                   0.07, 0.10, 0.30, 0.48, 0.54), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
oc <- sim_waterfall(target = 0.30, p_true = p_true, cohort_size = 3,
                    n_trials = 10000)
oc  # the selection of every combination and of the whole contour

When a subtrial ends without a candidate MTD, BOIN::get.oc.comb() drops its data from the counts; the package keeps them, and boin_compatible = TRUE drops them. A trial selects one combination at every level of drug A, so the results do not enter oc_results() and oc_compare(), which assume one selected dose per trial.

How the implementation is checked:

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhang2016.R sets the simulations beside Tables IV, V and S1 of Zhang and Yuan (2016): with boin_compatible = TRUE and the default seed of BOIN::get.oc.comb(), all 398 cells are equal to the printed digits.
  • With boin_compatible = TRUE and the same seed, all 870 values of inst/validation/compare-waterfall-with-BOIN.R, in 20 settings, are equal to those of BOIN::get.oc.comb().
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a transcription of BOIN::get.oc.comb() in Python, fed with the same random numbers.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-combination").

Optimal biological dose: the BOIN-ET design

For targeted and immune therapies the aim is often the optimal biological dose (OBD), which weighs the response against the toxicity, rather than the MTD. The BOIN-ET design of Takeda, Taguri and Morita (2018) decides the next dose from both the DLT rate and the response rate at the current dose, with boundaries lambda1, lambda2 and eta1 that minimize the probability of an incorrect decision, and selects the OBD at the end of the trial.

boin_et_decision_table(target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60, n = c(3, 6))

oc <- sim_boin_et(
  target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40),
  p_resp = c(0.05, 0.35, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

The rules follow the ‘boinet’ package (Yamaguchi, Takeda and Maruo, 2025), the reference implementation of the authors: the boundary search of boinet::gridoptim(), the admissibility of a dose re-derived after every cohort, and the estimators and selection rules of boinet::obd.select() (observed rates, model-averaged unimodal isotonic regression or fractional polynomial logistic regression; the highest response up to the estimated MTD or one of three utilities). The trial runs in C++ and the OBD selection too; the model-based estimates are computed once for every distinct set of final data. boin_et_select_obd() selects the OBD from completed trials.

Two rules differ from ‘boinet’, to keep to Takeda et al. (2018), who do not allow dose skipping during escalation: a dose excluded by its DLT data also excludes every higher dose, as in the later BF-BOIN-ET design of the same group, and an escalation from the highest dose ends the trial when that dose is excluded. boinet_compatible = TRUE applies the rules of ‘boinet’.

The time-to-event version, TITE-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2020), lets patients arrive while others are still assessed, and the backfill version, BF-BOIN-ET (Takeda, Zhu and Hirakawa, 2025), treats the patients who arrive in the meantime at lower doses with a promising response rate:

oc <- sim_tite_boin_et(
  target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.60,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40),
  p_resp = c(0.05, 0.35, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, window = 30, resp_window = 45,
  accrual_rate = 1 / 10, n_trials = 10000
)

oc_bf <- sim_bf_boin_et(
  target = 0.30, target_resp = 0.25,
  p_true = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.20, 0.22, 0.45),
  p_resp = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 0.68, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, window = 1, accrual_rate = 3,
  n_trials = 10000
)

The rules follow boinet::tite.boinet() and bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet().

How the implementation is checked:

  • The boundaries 0.14, 0.35 and 0.48 and the decision tables of Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2018) are reproduced exactly, and inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2018.R sets the simulations beside Table 3. inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2020.R does the same for Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2020), whose simulations did not wait for finished assessments (min_completed_share = 0), and inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2025.R for Tables 1 and 2 of Takeda et al. (2025). In scenario 11 of the 2018 and 2020 articles the tables print a response rate of 0.55 at the lowest dose and Figure 2 shows 0.05; the published results agree with 0.05, which the scripts use.
  • The tests compare the boundaries with boinet::gridoptim() and the OBD of simulated trials with boinet::obd.select(): the same dose is selected in every trial, except that doses whose utilities are equal as fractions tie here, where rounding error decides between them in ‘boinet’.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, fed with the same random numbers.
  • inst/validation/compare-with-boinet.R compares the operating characteristics with boinet::boinet() and boinet::tite.boinet(), and inst/validation/compare-with-bfboinet.R with bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet(). The packages draw their random numbers differently, so they agree in distribution, not trial by trial.
  • The TITE-BOIN-ET and BF-BOIN-ET engines agree exactly with separate Python implementations of the R code of ‘boinet’ and ‘bfboinet’.

For two drugs given together, sim_boin_etc() runs BOIN-ET in subtrials of the dose matrix, the BOIN-ETC design of Kakizume et al. (2024). inst/reproduce/reproduce_Kakizume2024.R compares it with the tables of the article and inst/validation/compare-with-BOINETC.R with the code of the authors.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-boin-et") for the decision rules, the selection of the OBD, the dose moves that differ from ‘boinet’, BOIN-ETC and the results of these checks.

Optimal biological dose from grades: gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET

The gBOIN-ET design of Takeda et al. (2022) is the BOIN-ET design for toxicity and efficacy outcomes with several categories that each carry a score: the mean scores at the current dose take the place of the DLT and response rates. Its time-to-event version, TITE-gBOIN-ET (Takeda et al., 2023), enrolls the next cohort while earlier patients are still assessed, with effective numbers of patients as in TITE-BOIN-ET.

p_grade <- rbind(                      # grades 0 or 1, 2, 3 and 4
  c(0.83, 0.75, 0.62, 0.51, 0.34, 0.19),
  c(0.12, 0.15, 0.18, 0.19, 0.16, 0.11),
  c(0.04, 0.07, 0.11, 0.14, 0.15, 0.11),
  c(0.01, 0.03, 0.09, 0.16, 0.35, 0.59)
)
p_resp_grade <- rbind(                 # SD or PD, PR and CR
  c(0.90, 0.70, 0.50, 0.30, 0.25, 0.20),
  c(0.05, 0.20, 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20),
  c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60)
)
oc <- sim_gboin_et(
  target = 0.47 / 1.5, target_resp = 0.95 / 1.5,
  p_grade = p_grade, p_resp_grade = p_resp_grade,
  score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), score_resp = c(0, 1, 1.5),
  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

oc_tite <- sim_tite_gboin_et(
  target = 0.47 / 1.5, target_resp = 0.95 / 1.5,
  p_grade = p_grade, p_resp_grade = p_resp_grade,
  score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), score_resp = c(0, 1, 1.5),
  n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3,
  window = 30, resp_window = 60, accrual_rate = 1 / 10,  # days
  n_trials = 10000
)

The rules follow boinet::gboinet() and boinet::tite.gboinet(), with the two changes described above for BOIN-ET; boinet_compatible = TRUE drops them. The selection of the optimal dose of Takeda et al. (2022), the linear fractional polynomial among the doses with at least six patients, is est_method = "fp_linear" with min_obd_sample = 6.

How the implementation is checked:

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2022.R reproduces the 12 boundaries printed in Takeda et al. (2022) and sets the simulations beside its Table 1, with the category probabilities that the program of the authors draws, which are not those tabulated: 119 of the 130 cells lie within simulation error, four are explained by rules of that program, and 7 do not agree for a reason that was not found. With boinet_compatible = TRUE, all 156 values of inst/validation/compare-with-gboinet.R agree with boinet::gboinet() within simulation error.
  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2023.R sets the simulations of TITE-gBOIN-ET beside Table 1 and Tables S2 to S6 of Takeda et al. (2023). The R program of the authors, written again in C++, reproduces its published summaries exactly; it moves to a lower dose at random in a case in which the design keeps a single dose, and excludes doses with the effective numbers of patients, which the article and boinet::tite.gboinet() do not. Of the 570 cells, 273 lie within simulation error and 297 are explained by these two points; against the program without them, all 570 lie within simulation error. With boinet_compatible = TRUE, all 168 values of inst/validation/compare-with-tite-gboinet.R agree with boinet::tite.gboinet() within simulation error.
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with separate implementations written in Python, fed with the same random numbers. With two categories scored 0 and 1 they are those of BOIN-ET and TITE-BOIN-ET.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-boin-et").

Optimal biological dose: the BOIN12 design

The BOIN12 design of Lin et al. (2020) scores each patient by a utility, 100 for a response without DLT, 0 for a DLT without response and two values in between elicited from the clinicians (40 and 60 by default). The next cohort goes to the dose, among the current one and its neighbors, whose utility is most likely to exceed a benchmark, after the BOIN boundaries have ruled out an escalation from a toxic dose. The desirabilities can be tabulated for the protocol:

boin12_decision_table(target = 0.35, target_resp = 0.25)

Here target is the highest acceptable DLT rate and target_resp the lowest acceptable response rate. The operating characteristics follow the same pattern as the other designs:

oc <- sim_boin12(
  target = 0.35, target_resp = 0.25,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.12, 0.27, 0.35, 0.50),
  p_resp = c(0.20, 0.35, 0.36, 0.37, 0.38),
  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

The table reproduces Table 3 of Lin et al. (2020) in all 166 cells (inst/reproduce/reproduce_Lin2020.R), and inst/validation/compare-with-escalation.R compares the operating characteristics with the BOIN12 design of the ‘escalation’ package.

The time-to-event version, TITE-BOIN12 (Zhou et al., 2022), treats new patients while the DLT or the response of earlier patients is still pending, replacing each pending outcome by its expectation given the time followed. The windows and the accrual rate are given in the same unit of time:

oc <- sim_tite_boin12(
  target = 0.35, target_resp = 0.25,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.12, 0.27, 0.35, 0.50),
  p_resp = c(0.20, 0.35, 0.36, 0.37, 0.38),
  n_cohort = 12, cohort_size = 3,
  window = 1.5, resp_window = 2, accrual_rate = 3,  # months
  n_trials = 10000
)
oc

inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2022.R compares the desirabilities of Table S.3 of the Supplement of Zhou et al. (2022) and the operating characteristics of BOIN12 and TITE-BOIN12 in their Figure 3.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-boin12") for the rules, the arguments that give the rules of the simulations of the articles, Comb-BOIN12 and TITE-Comb-BOIN12 for two drugs given together, a comparison of BOIN, BOIN-ET and BOIN12 on the same scenarios, and the results of these checks.

Optimal biological dose by a utility of the joint outcome: the U-BOIN design

The U-BOIN design of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019) runs the BOIN design until a dose has 12 patients (n_stage1), and then treats each cohort above the highest dose tried while the DLT rate observed there stays at or below the escalation boundary, and otherwise at the admissible dose with the largest posterior mean utility of the four outcomes of a patient. The OBD is selected by the same utility at the end of the trial. Here tox_upper is the highest acceptable DLT probability and resp_lower the lowest acceptable response probability.

uboin_utility_table(3, tox_upper = 0.30, resp_lower = 0.20)

oc <- sim_uboin(
  tox_upper = 0.30, resp_lower = 0.20,
  p_true = c(0.02, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60),
  p_resp = c(0.20, 0.65, 0.65, 0.65, 0.65),
  n_cohort = 18, cohort_size = 3, resp_assoc = 0.2, n_trials = 10000
)
oc

The article gives neither the priors of its toxicity and futility rules nor whether doses not yet tried can be assigned in stage II. Beta(1, 1) priors and the tried doses only reproduce its simulations and are the defaults; the decision tables of its supporting information are reproduced with prior_resp = c(0.05, 0.05). There is no reference implementation.

How the implementation is checked:

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2019.R sets the simulations beside Table 3 of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019) and Tables S8 and S9 of its supporting information: all 264 cells lie within simulation error, with the rates of Scenario 7 of Table S8 for Scenario 7 of Table 3 and with s1 = 12 for Table S8, with which the published results agree rather than with the printed rates and the s1 = 9 of the text. The boundaries and the utility tables of the article are reproduced, but for one misprinted boundary of Table 2, and the admissibility of Tables S4 to S6 with prior_resp = c(0.05, 0.05).
  • The simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, fed with the same random numbers.

See vignette("simFastBOIN-boin12").

Why the trials stop

boin_simulate() records a reason for every trial, and sim_boin() reports the distribution in stop_reason_percent.

Reason Meaning
lowest_dose_eliminated The lowest dose was eliminated for toxicity
lowest_dose_too_toxic The extrasafe rule stopped the trial at the lowest dose
n_earlystop Enough patients had accrued at the current dose
max_sample_size The maximum number of patients was reached
max_cohorts All planned cohorts were completed

Checking the agreement with the BOIN package yourself 

reference <- BOIN::get.oc(
  target = 0.30, p.true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60),
  ncohort = 20, cohortsize = 3, n.earlystop = 18, ntrial = 10000, seed = 6
)

ours <- sim_boin(
  target = 0.30, p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 20, cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 18, n_trials = 10000, seed = 6
)

all.equal(unname(ours$sel_percent), reference$selpercent)
all.equal(unname(ours$n_pts_dose), reference$npatients)
all.equal(unname(ours$n_tox_dose), reference$ntox)
all.equal(ours$percent_no_mtd, reference$percentstop)

Speed

The simulation engines are written in C++. Measured on one Windows laptop with the settings and the numbers of trials of the comparisons in inst/validation/ and inst/reproduce/, the package ran the eleven designs that were compared with a reference implementation, in another R package or in the code of their authors, between about 8 and 11,000 times faster than the reference. For the setting of the previous section, 10,000 trials took 0.031 seconds with sim_boin() and 8 seconds with BOIN::get.oc(). The other designs ran 10,000 trials in less than a second, except Comb-BOIN12 and TITE-Comb-BOIN12, which take about 80 seconds with their default logistic estimate of the response rates. The article Computation time gives the times of every design, and inst/benchmark/benchmark.R measures them on your own machine.

Comparing with the 3+3 design

The traditional 3+3 design is included as a comparator. Its operating characteristics are obtained in closed form rather than by simulation, so they carry no Monte Carlo error.

oc_3p3(p_true = c(0.30, 0.48, 0.67))

# The other definition of the MTD in common use
oc_3p3(p_true = c(0.30, 0.48, 0.67), mtd_rule = "expand")

sim_3p3() simulates the same design and exists to confirm the closed form. The result of either has the same component names as the result of sim_boin(), so the two designs can be tabulated side by side.

decision_table_3p3() shows the rule itself, with print() and plot() methods like those of the BOIN decision table. oc_compare() judges the 3+3 and BOIN designs against the true MTDs of oc_scenarios(), as shown in the section “Tables and figures” of vignette("simFastBOIN-introduction").

decision_table_3p3(mtd_rule = "expand")

Upgrading from version 1.3.2

Version 2.0.0 renames most functions, changes the argument order of sim_boin() and corrects several defects that affected numerical results. Simulations run with the same seed will not reproduce the version 1.3.2 output. See NEWS.md for the full list and the mapping of old names to new ones.
